analogy.p: Imagine a doorman. An AND door says 'you may enter only if you have a ticket AND you are on the guest list', so both must be true. An OR door says 'you may enter if you have a ticket OR a staff pass', so either is enough. A NOT rule says 'you may enter if you are NOT wearing a hat', so it admits the opposite of the condition. This maps well onto the three gates and their truth tables. It breaks down because a real doorman might be flexible or make exceptions, whereas a logic gate follows its rule exactly every single time and only knows 1 and 0.

bullets: **Know** what AND, OR and NOT each do, in words and as a truth table.
**Recognise and draw** the standard gate symbols for AND, OR and NOT.
**Write** simple Boolean expressions such as Q = A AND B or Q = NOT A.
**Know** that every input and output is either **0** or **1** (also called False and True, or off and on).
**Apply** the operators to a short scenario by choosing the correct operator from the wording.
**Link** Boolean logic to IF statements, where AND, OR and NOT combine conditions.
This is a high-reliability topic: the facts are small, so learn them completely and practise drawing the symbols.
core.p: OCR J277 section 2.4 (Boolean logic) expects you to know and use the three basic logic operators AND, OR and NOT. You must recognise and draw the logic gate symbol for each, write simple Boolean expressions using them, and know exactly what output each one gives for every possible input. This note covers the three operators and their symbols; the companion note covers building full truth tables and combining gates into larger circuits. Boolean logic is examined in Paper 2 (Computational thinking, algorithms and programming) and questions are very predictable, so precise recall earns almost guaranteed marks.

bullets: A **Boolean value** has exactly two possible states: True/False, 1/0, on/off, high/low voltage.
A **logic gate** is an electronic component that takes one or more Boolean inputs and produces one Boolean output according to a fixed rule.
The rule for each gate is completely described by its **truth table**.
Gates are made from **transistors**, which act as electronic switches.
Combining gates into a **logic circuit** lets a computer carry out calculations and decisions, for example the adder circuits inside the arithmetic logic unit (ALU).
Boolean logic is the same idea you use in programming when a condition is True or False.
WHY it matters: because only two states are needed, hardware is simple, fast and reliable and less affected by electrical noise than a circuit with many voltage levels.
core.h: Boolean logic: what it is and why computers use it
core.p: Boolean logic is a form of logic in which every statement can only be **True or False**. It is named after the mathematician George Boole. In a computer these two values are represented by the two binary digits **1 (True)** and **0 (False)**, which in hardware are two voltage levels: a high voltage for 1 and a low voltage for 0. Computers are built from millions of tiny electronic switches called **transistors**, and a transistor is either conducting or not, so it naturally stores and processes only two states. Groups of transistors wired together form **logic gates**, and gates are combined to build every part of the CPU, including the circuits that add numbers and make decisions.

bullets: Expression: **Q = A AND B**.
Truth table: 0 AND 0 = 0, 0 AND 1 = 0, 1 AND 0 = 0, **1 AND 1 = 1**.
Only **one row out of four** gives an output of 1.
In plain English: the output is 1 only if A is 1 **and** B is 1.
Symbol: flat back, curved front, like a capital D; inputs on the straight edge.
Everyday example: a car will only start if the key is turned AND the brake pedal is pressed.
An AND gate can have more than two inputs; the output is 1 only if every one of them is 1.
Memory trick: AND is strict, so one 0 anywhere makes the answer 0.
core.p: The **AND** operator outputs 1 (True) only when **all of its inputs are 1**. If even one input is 0, the output is 0. A good way to remember it: a statement joined with AND is only true if both parts are true. With two inputs, A and B, the Boolean expression is written **Q = A AND B**, where Q is the output. In the logic gate symbol, AND looks like a capital D lying on its flat side: a straight back with a curved front and two input lines on the left. AND is used when a decision needs several conditions to all be met.

bullets: Expression: **Q = A OR B**.
Truth table: **0 OR 0 = 0**, 0 OR 1 = 1, 1 OR 0 = 1, 1 OR 1 = 1.
Three rows out of four give an output of 1; only the all-zero row gives 0.
In plain English: the output is 1 if A is 1 **or** B is 1 **or both**.
Symbol: curved back and a pointed front that curves to a tip on the right.
Everyday example: a house alarm sounds if the front door sensor OR the window sensor is triggered.
Do not confuse OR with the symbol for AND; AND has a flat back, OR has a curved back.
Memory trick: OR is generous, so one 1 anywhere makes the answer 1.
core.p: The **OR** operator outputs 1 (True) when **at least one input is 1**. It only gives 0 when every input is 0. In Boolean logic OR is **inclusive**, which means it is also true when both inputs are 1; this differs from everyday speech, where 'tea or coffee' often means one but not both. The expression with two inputs is **Q = A OR B**. The OR gate symbol has a curved back, like a shield or a crescent shape pointing to the right, and two input lines entering the curved side. OR is used when any one of several conditions is enough to trigger an outcome.

bullets: Expression: **Q = NOT A**.
Truth table: **NOT 0 = 1** and **NOT 1 = 0**.
It has **one input and one output**, unlike AND and OR which normally have two inputs.
Alternative name: **inverter**, because it inverts (flips) the value.
Symbol: a **triangle with a small circle** at the point.
NOT only changes the signal it is directly attached to, not the whole circuit.
NOT NOT A returns to A, because flipping twice gives the original value.
Everyday example: a light that turns on when it is NOT daylight.
core.p: The **NOT** operator has only **one input** and reverses it: NOT 0 = 1 and NOT 1 = 0. This is why it is also called an **inverter**. It is written **Q = NOT A**. The NOT gate symbol is a triangle pointing to the right with a **small circle (bubble) on the output**. The circle is the part that shows inversion, and examiners expect it. NOT is often used together with AND or OR to express conditions such as 'the door is open and the alarm is NOT switched off'.

bullets: **AND**: straight vertical back edge, curved front, two inputs on the left, one output on the right.
**OR**: curved back edge (the input side bows inward), curved sides meeting at a point on the right.
**NOT**: triangle with a small circle on the tip; **one** input only.
Draw each gate large enough to attach wires clearly; cramped drawings lose marks.
Label every input (A, B, C) and the final output (Q) exactly as the question does.
When one input feeds two gates, draw a **dot** at the junction so it is clear the wires connect.
Wires that cross without a dot do **not** connect.
Draw signals flowing left to right so the diagram is easy to mark.
core.h: Logic gate symbols: drawing them correctly
core.p: OCR questions regularly ask you to draw a logic diagram or to name a gate from its picture. Inputs are drawn on the **left** and the output on the **right**, with straight lines for wires. Label the inputs with letters such as A and B and the output with Q. Using the right shape matters because each mark is awarded for a correctly shaped gate with its connections. Practise drawing each gate until you can do it neatly in a few seconds, using a ruler for the wires if you can.

bullets: Use the exact output letter given (usually **Q**) on the left of the equals sign.
Write operators in capitals as words: **AND, OR, NOT**.
Put **NOT** directly in front of the thing it inverts, e.g. NOT A or NOT (A AND B).
Use **brackets** to make the order clear, e.g. A AND (NOT B).
Check an expression by testing one or two input combinations in your head.
Words in a scenario give clues: **'and', 'both', 'all'** suggest AND; **'or', 'either', 'any'** suggest OR; **'not', 'only if no', 'unless'** suggest NOT.
The number of gates in the diagram equals the number of operators in the expression.
core.p: A **Boolean expression** is a way of describing the output of a circuit in terms of its inputs, using the operators AND, OR and NOT. On OCR papers the operators are written as words, for example Q = A AND B or Q = (A AND B) OR C. Brackets show which part is worked out first. You may be asked to write an expression for a diagram, or for a scenario written in words, so you need to be comfortable moving between all three: words, expressions and diagrams.

bullets: Order: **1 brackets, 2 NOT, 3 AND, 4 OR**.
A OR B AND C is the same as A OR (B AND C), not (A OR B) AND C.
NOT A AND B means (NOT A) AND B; NOT applies only to A unless brackets say otherwise.
NOT (A AND B) is different from NOT A AND NOT B; the brackets change the meaning.
Always work out the innermost brackets first.
Adding extra brackets never costs marks and often prevents errors.
In a diagram the order is shown by the layout: gates closer to the inputs are evaluated first.
core.h: Order of operations in Boolean expressions
core.p: When an expression contains more than one operator, there is a standard order of evaluation, similar to BIDMAS in maths. Anything in **brackets** is worked out first. Then **NOT** is applied, then **AND**, and finally **OR**. So the expression A OR B AND C means A OR (B AND C), because AND is evaluated before OR. This is a common source of mistakes, so in your own answers always add brackets to remove any doubt. Examiners will accept brackets that make your meaning clearer.

bullets: **AND**: outputs 0, 0, 0, **1** for inputs 00, 01, 10, 11.
**NOT**: outputs 1, 0 for input 0, 1.
Number of rows = 2^n, where n is the number of inputs (2 inputs = 4 rows, 3 inputs = 8 rows).
Use the same order of rows every time (counting up in binary).
A truth table proves the behaviour for **all** cases, not just one example.
Compare AND and OR: they differ in only the middle two rows (01 and 10) and the first and last rows are the same.
The two tables with highlighted 1s should look like a pattern you can sketch from memory.
core.p: A **truth table** lists every possible combination of inputs and the output each gives. For a gate with n inputs there are **2 to the power n** rows, so a one-input NOT gate has 2 rows and a two-input AND or OR gate has 4 rows. Each of the three basic truth tables must be memorised. You should list the input combinations in the standard binary counting order, 00, 01, 10, 11, so that none is missed or repeated and so the marker can check it quickly.

bullets: Closed switch = 1, open switch = 0; lamp lit = output 1.
**Series switches = AND**: both must be closed to complete the circuit.
**Parallel switches = OR**: either closed switch completes a path to the lamp.
A switch that turns the lamp **off** when pressed behaves like **NOT**.
Transistors are tiny switches controlled by an electrical signal rather than a hand.
A CPU contains billions of transistors wired into gates.
This analogy only explains the simple gates; real gates work with voltage levels rather than mechanical contacts.
core.h: From switches to gates: a physical picture
core.p: You can picture logic gates as electrical switches controlling a lamp. If two switches are wired **in series** (one after the other), current flows only if both are closed, which is exactly the AND rule. If two switches are wired **in parallel** (on separate paths), current flows if either is closed, which is the OR rule. A normally closed switch or relay that opens when pressed behaves like a NOT. This picture helps you understand why the rules are what they are, and it is the basis of real computer hardware where transistors act as the switches.

bullets: if age >= 13 AND age <= 19 then is True only when both comparisons are True.
if day == "Sat" OR day == "Sun" then is True if either is True.
if NOT finished then runs when the Boolean variable finished is False.
Comparison operators such as <, >, ==, != produce True/False values that AND, OR, NOT can combine.
A common logic error is using **OR** where **AND** is needed in a range check (age < 13 OR age > 19 is the opposite of what is wanted).
Boolean variables store True or False and are used as flags.
Selection (if/else) and iteration (while) both rely on Boolean conditions.
Beyond the specification: De Morgan's laws show that NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B), but you are not required to know them.
core.p: The same three operators appear in program code when you combine conditions in an IF statement or a loop. In OCR reference language and most high-level languages the words **AND, OR and NOT** are used. A condition such as age >= 13 AND age <= 19 evaluates to True only if both parts are True. A condition using OR is True if either part is True, and NOT reverses a True or False result. Understanding the truth tables therefore helps you predict what a program will do and find logic errors, a common exam task.

bullets: Step 1: list the **inputs** and give each a letter (C = cold, W = window open).
Step 2: say what the **output** is (H = heater on).
Step 3: highlight the connecting words: **and, or, not, unless, either, both**.
Step 4: write the expression and add brackets if it is not obvious.
Step 5: test it using a real situation: cold and window closed should give heater on.
Step 6: draw the logic diagram if required, with labelled inputs and output.
Make sure NOT is attached to the correct input: 'window not open' means NOT W.
Check that the circuit does not give the output in situations that should be off.
core.h: Solving problems: from scenario to expression
core.p: Many questions describe a real situation and ask for the Boolean expression or the diagram. Work methodically. First, identify the **inputs** and give each a letter. Then decide what combination makes the output 1. Look for the key words that signal AND, OR or NOT. Finally write the expression, check it with an example, and draw it. For instance, 'a greenhouse heater turns on if it is cold and the window is not open' becomes H = C AND NOT W, with C meaning cold and W meaning the window is open.

bullets: **Alarms**: sound if (door sensor OR window sensor) AND system armed.
**Washing machine**: motor on if door closed AND water level correct.
**Vending machine**: dispense if enough money AND item selected.
**CPU/ALU**: adders, comparators and control circuits are built from gates.
**Search engines/databases**: AND narrows results, OR widens them, NOT excludes.
**Programs**: IF statements combine conditions with the same operators.
The same small set of gates can build any digital circuit, which is why they are fundamental.
core.h: Real-world uses of AND, OR and NOT
core.p: Logic gates are everywhere, which is why this topic is on the specification. Security systems use AND and OR to decide when to sound an alarm, vending machines use AND to check that enough money is inserted and an item is selected, and a washing machine uses AND to make sure the door is shut and water is in before the drum turns. Inside the CPU, combinations of gates add binary numbers, compare values and decide which instruction to run next. Search engines use the same operators: searching for cats AND dogs returns pages with both, cats OR dogs returns pages with either, and cats NOT dogs excludes pages mentioning dogs.

bullets: **Binary**: one bit is a Boolean value; logic gates operate on bits.
**CPU/ALU**: the arithmetic logic unit performs logical operations using gates.
**Programming**: conditions in IF, WHILE and REPEAT use Boolean expressions.
**Algorithms**: flowchart decision boxes ask Boolean questions with Yes/No outcomes.
**Testing**: boundary data tests the edges of AND/OR range checks.
**Databases/SQL**: WHERE clauses combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT.
**Next step**: truth tables for combined circuits and drawing multi-gate diagrams, covered in the truth tables note.
core.p: Boolean logic connects to many parts of the OCR J277 course. It links to binary and data representation, since a single bit is one Boolean value. It links to the CPU, because the ALU is made of logic circuits. It links to programming, because selection and iteration use Boolean conditions, and to computational thinking, because decomposing a decision into True/False tests is a form of abstraction. Making these links in longer answers shows depth and can help you structure extended responses.

exam: **Command words**: 'State' and 'Give' need a short fact (e.g. the output of an AND gate for inputs 1 and 0); 'Complete' means fill in a table; 'Draw' means a labelled diagram; 'Describe' needs a clear rule.
**1 mark**: name the gate from its symbol, or give the output for one input combination. Use the exact words AND, OR or NOT.
**2 marks**: complete a short truth table (often 1 mark for the first correct rows and 1 for the rest) or write a simple expression such as Q = A AND B.
**Model phrase for AND**: 'The output is 1 only when both inputs are 1.' For OR: 'The output is 1 when at least one input is 1.' For NOT: 'The output is the opposite of the input.'
**Drawing questions**: label the inputs and output, draw each gate with the correct shape, use ruled lines, and put a dot at junctions.
**Scenario questions**: underline the key words 'and', 'or', 'not' in the question, then build the expression from them.
**Truth table checking**: after completing a table, check that AND has exactly one 1 and OR has exactly one 0 in a two-input table.
**Programming links**: you may be asked to say whether a condition is True or False for given values; evaluate each part separately then combine with AND/OR/NOT.
Always write answers in the answer lines using 0 and 1 (not True/False) unless the question says otherwise.
Do not waste time: these are quick marks. Learn the three tables and three shapes thoroughly and you will rarely drop a mark.
If a question says 'explain' why a circuit gives a certain output, refer to specific inputs and the rule, for example 'both inputs are 1 so the AND gate outputs 1'.

mistakes.r: OR is inclusive: 1 OR 1 = 1. The output is 0 only when both inputs are 0.
mistakes.w: Writing 0 for OR when both inputs are 1 (treating OR as 'one or the other').

mistakes.r: A NOT gate is a triangle with a circle on the output and has exactly one input.
mistakes.w: Drawing a NOT gate without the small circle, or with two inputs.

mistakes.r: AND has a flat (straight) back; OR has a curved back.
mistakes.w: Mixing up AND and OR symbols, e.g. drawing a curved back for AND.

mistakes.r: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, so only the row 11 gives 1.
mistakes.w: Giving the AND truth table output as 1 for the rows 01 and 10.

mistakes.r: NOT is applied before AND, so NOT A AND B means (NOT A) AND B. Use brackets to show what you mean.
mistakes.w: Writing NOT A AND B and meaning NOT (A AND B).

mistakes.r: List every combination once, in binary counting order: 00, 01, 10, 11.
mistakes.w: Leaving out or repeating input combinations in a truth table.

mistakes.r: NOT reverses the input value: NOT 1 = 0 and NOT 0 = 1.
mistakes.w: Saying that NOT 'changes the gate' or 'cancels' the input.

mistakes.r: Write the operators as AND, OR and NOT in the expression, as used in OCR papers.
mistakes.w: Using 'and/or' language, or symbols like + and x, in the expression instead of the words required.

mistakes.r: Draw a dot where wires join; wires crossing without a dot are not connected.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the dot at a junction, or letting wires cross with no clear connection.

summary: Know what the Boolean operators AND, OR and NOT do, draw their gate symbols, write simple Boolean expressions and give the output of each operator for every input. It matters because every digital circuit and every program condition is built from these three ideas.

terms.d: A data type or logic system with only two possible values: True or False (1 or 0).
An electronic component that takes one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output according to a logical rule.
A Boolean operator that outputs 1 only when all of its inputs are 1.
A Boolean operator that outputs 1 when at least one of its inputs is 1 (inclusive OR).
A Boolean operator with a single input that outputs the opposite value: 1 becomes 0 and 0 becomes 1.
Another name for a NOT gate, because it inverts its input.
A binary value (0 or 1) fed into a logic gate or circuit, usually labelled A, B, C.
The binary value produced by a gate or circuit, usually labelled Q.
A table that shows the output of a logic circuit for every possible combination of inputs.
A statement using operators such as AND, OR and NOT that describes the output of a logic circuit.
A drawing of a logic circuit using standard gate symbols joined by wires.
A combination of logic gates connected together so the output of one can be the input of another.
A tiny electronic switch, used to build logic gates, that is either on or off.
A symbol or word, such as AND, OR or NOT, that acts on one or more values to produce a result.
A single 0 or 1, the smallest unit of data, which can represent one Boolean value.
A Boolean expression in a program, such as age >= 13, that evaluates to True or False.
The meaning of OR in Boolean logic: true if one input or both inputs are true.
The order in which operators are evaluated: brackets, then NOT, then AND, then OR.

worked.ans: (a) H = C AND NOT W (1 mark). (b) C,W: 0,0 gives H = 0; 0,1 gives 0; 1,0 gives 1; 1,1 gives 0 (3 marks). The heater is on only when it is cold with the window closed.
worked.q: A greenhouse heater H switches on when it is cold (C) AND the window is NOT open (W). (a) Write a Boolean expression for H. (b) Complete a truth table for H. [4]
steps: Identify inputs: C = 1 if cold; W = 1 if window open. Output: H = 1 if heater on.
'Cold AND window NOT open' gives H = C AND NOT W.
Rows in order of C, W: 00, 01, 10, 11.
Row 00: NOT W = 1, C AND 1 = 0 AND 1 = 0.
Row 10: NOT W = 1, so H = 1 AND 1 = 1.

worked.ans: (a) An AND gate outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1; with A = 1, B = 0 the output is 0. (b) An OR gate outputs 1 when at least one input is 1; with A = 1, B = 0 the output is 1. (c) A NOT gate outputs the opposite of its input; with A = 1 the output is 0. (1 mark for each rule and 1 mark for each correct value.)
worked.q: Describe the output of (a) an AND gate, (b) an OR gate and (c) a NOT gate. State the output when A = 1 and B = 0 for the AND and OR gates, and when A = 1 for the NOT gate. [6]
steps: AND: 1 only if both inputs are 1. For A = 1, B = 0 not both are 1, so output 0.
OR: 1 if at least one input is 1. For A = 1, B = 0 one input is 1, so output 1.
NOT: reverses the input. For A = 1, output is 0.

worked.ans: (a) True, both parts are True. (b) False, because 12 is not >= 13 and AND needs both parts True. (c) False, because 20 is not <= 19 so one part is False.
worked.q: A program contains: IF age >= 13 AND age <= 19 THEN. State whether the condition is True or False when age is (a) 15, (b) 12, (c) 20. Explain your answers. [3]
steps: (a) 15 >= 13 is True and 15 <= 19 is True. True AND True = True.
(b) 12 >= 13 is False. False AND anything = False.
(c) 20 >= 13 is True but 20 <= 19 is False. True AND False = False.
